about: Lenses for the Workshop: ways poets have made songs, each a way to make a version of a caryā without breaking its shape (one English line per half-line, the refrain the same every time, the signature couplet kept). A lens sets the mixing board (0 cool .. 1 hot on lineation, syntax, rhythm, rhyme) and says how the English moves inside that shape. Each names its tradition: english, sufi, zen, shakespeare or bardic. Touchstones are public-domain lines only (originals, or translations published before 1929). See research/western-lenses.md, research/sufi-poets.md, research/zen-mountain-poets.md, research/shakespeare-sonnets.md and research/bardic-tradition.md.

lenses.name: Blake
lenses.after: after William Blake, Songs of Innocence and of Experience (1789–94)
lenses.how: Rhymed couplets of four beats, in plain words of one or two syllables. Lines that end on their stress, closing like a door. Paradox stated flat, never explained; a question asked and left hanging. The voice of a child or a prophet who does not trust priests.
lenses.why: Blake called his books illuminated printing: word and picture etched on one copper plate and coloured by hand. His Songs are the English tradition's nearest kin to the siddhas: short sung poems of vision against the temple, in couplets.
lenses.touchstone: Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night
lenses.suits: the teaching songs, the riddles, a refrain that must ring

lenses.name: Ballad
lenses.after: after the Child ballads (the old songs of Scotland and the English border)
lenses.how: Lines of four beats and three, rhymed on the short line. The refrain stitched between the lines as the ballads stitch in theirs. The story told in leaps, without explaining how one scene becomes the next. Incremental repetition: a line comes back changed by a word or two.
lenses.why: The ballad refrain ("Binnorie, O Binnorie") is the English twin of the caryā's ধ্রু: a line the singers come back to after every verse, whatever happens in it.
lenses.suits: songs with a story, a woman's name struck again and again, a sudden turn

lenses.name: Dickinson
lenses.after: after Emily Dickinson's hymn-metre riddles
lenses.how: Hymn metre (eight syllables, then six, alternating, four beats then three). Slant rhyme, never a chime too sweet. Dashes that cut the syntax where the breath catches. Riddles put as definitions ("X is Y"). The strange thing kept strange and very close.
lenses.why: Dickinson made a private, riddling, ecstatic poetry out of the plainest church tune, as the siddhas made theirs out of the plainest folk song. Her slant rhyme is the honest rhyme English can afford.
lenses.suits: the twilight-language riddles, paradox, the inward songs

lenses.name: Psalm
lenses.after: after the King James Psalms (1611) and Hebrew parallelism
lenses.how: Each line in two halves around a pause, the second echoing, answering or sharpening the first. No rhyme and no count of beats: the thought rhymes instead. A refrain answered by the congregation after every verse, word for word. Long, grave, open lines.
lenses.why: Robert Lowth (1753) showed that Hebrew poetry rhymes in thought, not sound, which is why the Psalms survive translation. The caryā couplet, a statement and its answer, can be heard the same way.
lenses.touchstone: O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
lenses.suits: the rapt songs, a refrain like a response, the grave teaching

lenses.name: Hopkins
lenses.after: after Gerard Manley Hopkins (poems 1918)
lenses.how: Sprung rhythm: count only the stresses and let them crowd together. Alliteration and chimes inside the line; words struck against each other ("sky-scoop"). Compounds made on the spot. Ecstatic, packed, sensuous; syntax that bends to the stress.
lenses.why: Hopkins heard the world's things each 'selving', flashing out their own being; the caryā's objects (oars, the sky-scoop, the lotus root) ask to be heard that hard.
lenses.touchstone: As kingfishers catch fire, dragonflies draw flame
lenses.suits: songs dense with objects, the boat songs, ecstasy

lenses.name: Cathay
lenses.after: after Ezra Pound's Cathay (1915)
lenses.how: Plain statement. One image to a line, the line closed. No rhyme, no ornament, no explaining; feeling held back and left to the images. Short sentences side by side. Proper names kept as they are.
lenses.why: Pound made Cathay from Ernest Fenollosa's word-by-word notes on Chinese poems he could not read: the English tradition's great example of poems made from a gloss. This edition's word-by-word gloss is that notebook.
lenses.suits: any song, as the cool pole: to hear what the images do alone

lenses.name: Work song
lenses.after: after the sea shanties and work songs of call and response
lenses.how: A caller's line and the crew's answer. The beat of the oar stroke or the hauling rope: every line on the same strong four. The refrain after every verse, sung back exactly. Commands, names, calls. Rhyme where it falls easily; repetition always.
lenses.why: The ferry songs are rowing songs: "Row, Ḍombī, row". Work songs keep a crew together by the same means the caryā keeps its hearers: the call, the answer, the return.
lenses.suits: the boat and ferry songs, commands, refrains

lenses.name: Owen
lenses.after: after Wilfred Owen's para rhyme (poems 1920)
lenses.how: Para rhyme: keep the consonants of the word you would rhyme and change its vowel (hall, hell), so the ear expects a chime and gets a shudder. Steady, heavy lines. Plain words; the horror left in the thing itself.
lenses.why: Owen used the coldest rhyme there is for the trenches. The caryās have their threats and their terrors, where a sweet rhyme would lie; but their charnel ground is the tantric yogi's own intimate place, and there the cold chime can lie instead.
lenses.suits: threat and horror: the fierce songs, a sudden threat, the kāpālika's menace. Not every cremation-ground image: where a song is at home among the bones, para rhyme is the wrong temperature

lenses.name: Ghazal
lenses.after: after the Persian ghazal of Rumi and Hafez, and Agha Shahid Ali's ghazals in English (2000–2003)
lenses.how: Close the second line of every couplet on one end-phrase, the radif, with a different rhyme word just before it each time; the first couplet closes both its lines on it. Take the radif from the song itself, the name or word it strikes most, set where the line holds it or can hold it by reordering, never brought in from outside. Keep each couplet closed on itself, and let address, command, question and 'I said… he said' carry it where the song has them. The refrain stays word for word. The signature couplet speaks as the ghazal's signature does, the singer summing himself up, rebuking or consoling, but keeps the song's person: 'Lūyī says', never 'O Lūyī'.
lenses.why: The radif is the Persian tradition's absolute rhyme: the refrain folded into the end of the line, where the mystical poet can go on repeating one name. The signature in the last couplet is the ghazal's bhaṇitā, turned inward. Both carry into English: Dick Davis finds the radif often transferable, and Agha Shahid Ali proved it.
lenses.touchstone: man ghulām-i qamar-am, ghayr-i qamar hīch magū
lenses.suits: songs that strike one name or word again and again (song 10's Ḍombī), the addressed and rapt songs, a song whose last couplet signs

lenses.name: Masnavi couplets
lenses.after: after Rumi's Masnavi (1258–73), and its English in Whinfield (1898) and Nicholson (1926)
lenses.how: Rhyme each couplet on its own sound (aa bb cc), both lines on one steady measure: the caryā already rhymes couplet by couplet, so keep its rhymes and bring them to a full chime where English honestly can. Where the song commands its hearer, command as plainly ('listen'); where a thing in the song speaks, let it say 'I'; add no speaker and no hearer the song lacks. Lay saying beside story, and where the song strikes a plain word at a couplet's end, strike it there each time. The refrain stays word for word, the signature keeps 'says', and the last line lands short and plain.
lenses.why: The Masnavi teaches in couplets that rhyme two by two, and fifteen of its opening eighteen couplets end on a repeated word. A caryā rhymes the same way, couplet by couplet: it rhymes like a masnavi and signs like a ghazal.
lenses.touchstone: Listen to the reed how it tells a tale, complaining of separations
lenses.suits: the teaching songs, songs in which a thing speaks or is spoken to (the boat, the oar, the hut), the parables

lenses.name: Rubai
lenses.after: after the Persian quatrain and FitzGerald's Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám (1859)
lenses.how: Hear each couplet with the refrain sung after it as one quatrain rhymed a a b a. The couplet's two lines rhyme together and on the refrain's closing sound; the refrain's first line stays unrhymed, the held breath, and its second line is the turn that closes hard. The refrain stays word for word, so the couplets do the rhyming, honestly or not at all. One steady measure (FitzGerald's five beats), plain words, a paradox stated and not explained. The signature keeps 'says'.
lenses.why: The rubai is the Persian tradition's shortest whole poem and its aphorism, and FitzGerald kept its aaba and made English poems of it. A caryā couplet with its refrain after it is four lines that can turn in the last.
lenses.touchstone: Awake! for Morning in the Bowl of Night
lenses.suits: the riddles, a paradox that turns in the last line, a refrain whose closing sound can carry the song

lenses.name: Cold Mountain
lenses.after: after Hanshan (Cold Mountain) and the Chan hermit poets
lenses.how: Plain spoken English, low and colloquial, each line a closed sentence of about the same length. Where the song has an 'I' and a 'you', let them talk plainly, and put the song's own questions straight; add none. Where the song mocks the learned, laugh as bluntly; no ornament, no doctrine explained. Rhyme lightly on a couplet's second line, or not at all. The refrain stays word for word, and the signature keeps 'says' in a street voice, as Hanshan names himself: 'Hanshan puts out these words'.
lenses.why: Hanshan wrote freer ancient-style verse in more colloquial language than almost any Tang poet, signed his poems with the mountain he lived on, and mocked the scholar who said he could not keep the tones. The siddhas sang in the vernacular too, and signed their songs.
lenses.touchstone: 人問寒山道，寒山路不通
lenses.suits: the signed songs, the songs that mock pandits, riddles put to the listener

lenses.name: Parallel couplet
lenses.after: after the middle couplets of Tang regulated verse (對仗)
lenses.how: Set a couplet's two lines on one frame wherever the song's two half-lines already pair: noun answers noun, verb answers verb, place answers place, in the same order; creature against creature, stillness against sound. Close each line, with no 'and' between them: the pairing is the join. Where the song strikes a word twice, strike it twice. Never force a pair the song does not make; a couplet that tells a story stays a story. The refrain stays word for word, and the signature keeps 'says'.
lenses.why: Regulated verse required its middle couplets to be parallel, and Kao and Mei call parallelism a grammatical equivalence, as rhyme is a phonetic one. It survives translation when sound does not, and a caryā couplet is often a statement and its answer.
lenses.touchstone: Drawing sword, cut into water, water again flow: / Raise cup, quench sorrow, sorrow again sorry.
lenses.suits: paired images (the two rivers, sun and moon), paradox, the refrain couplet

lenses.name: Haiku cut
lenses.after: after Bashō's hokku and the cutting word (kireji)
lenses.how: Inside each couplet, set the song's two things side by side with one cut between them and nothing to join them: no 'like', no 'as', no 'because'. The cut is a line's end, a dash or a colon. Concrete things of one moment, short lines, uncounted; where the song gives a motion or a sound, let it come after the cut. Add no 'I' and no one to hear. The refrain stays whole, and the signature keeps 'says'.
lenses.why: The kireji both cuts and joins: two centres, and an equation the listener must make. Bashō's frog jumps where the tradition had it sing. A caryā image set against the next without the commentary's bridge asks the same of its hearer.
lenses.touchstone: furuike ya / kawazu tobikomu / mizu no oto
lenses.suits: single images, the moment before a turn, a couplet cut to its two centres

lenses.name: Shakespearean sonnet
lenses.after: after Shakespeare's Sonnets (1609), above all Sonnet 29
lenses.how: Five-beat lines, rhymed as the sonnet rhymes: alternate rhymes across two couplets (abab), the song's last couplet rhymed on itself. Let the syntax think: where the song's grammar allows, hold a main verb back and lay the trouble out in phrases side by side before it. Turn where the song turns, on one word ('yet', 'but'), as hard as it turns; the sonnet's own places, line 9 and the couplet, never move it. Where the song strikes a word again, let each return mean something new; an identity stays an identity, never a 'like'. The refrain stays word for word, and the signature keeps 'says'.
lenses.why: The English sonnet was born as translation: Wyatt made his from Petrarch, keeping the images and changing the ending. It is English's form for a mind that turns, as song 10 turns from courting Ḍombī to killing her, and its cool, thinking syntax under hot sound is a gap no other lens gives.
lenses.touchstone: Like to the lark at break of day arising / From sullen earth, sings hymns at heaven's gate
lenses.suits: songs that turn hard, a key word struck again with a new sense, a song that thinks in one long sentence

lenses.name: Bardic
lenses.after: after the classical Irish court poets (c. 1250–1650) and the deibhidhe
lenses.how: Count syllables, not stresses: seven to every line, each couplet closing its sense. Rhyme each couplet the deibhidhe way, a stressed last word against an unstressed tail one syllable longer (Hugh / curfew). Give every line two alliterating words and, where the song allows, a word inside one line rhyming with a word inside the next. If the song's last line can honestly end on the song's first word, end it there and shut the poem (the dúnadh); if it cannot, say so. The refrain stays word for word, and the signature keeps 'says'.
lenses.why: The dúnadh is the refrain folded into a circle: the poem's first word comes back once, at the end, and shuts it. The bardic quatrain, like the caryā couplet, must make sense on its own, and its rhyme by consonant class runs hotter in pattern than English perfect rhyme.
lenses.touchstone: Messe ocus Pangur Bán · cechtar nathar fria saindan
lenses.suits: the teaching songs, a song that should close on its first word

lenses.name: Keen
lenses.after: after the caoineadh: the keening women and Eibhlín Dubh Ní Chonaill's lament (1773)
lenses.how: Short lines of two or three beats, one to each half-line. Where the song calls someone, let the call open the couplet and come back changed by a word each time, as the keen's 'my friend' does; add no call the song lacks. Carry one stressed vowel through a couplet, and where the grammar allows end its two lines on the same small word (you, you; with you, with you). Keep every thing the song names exactly, the body too. The refrain comes back whole, like the keeners' cry, and the signature keeps 'says'.
lenses.why: The keen is improvised over the body and remembered by the women who heard it. Its returning address is a ধ্রু made of grief, and its word for the cry (faíd) is the one Old Irish uses for a bird's call.
lenses.suits: the songs of loss and parting, a woman's voice, a name called again and again

lenses.name: Gleeman
lenses.after: after Michael Moran, 'Zozimus' (d. 1846), the blind reciter of the Dublin streets
lenses.how: Rhymed couplets, perfect rhyme where it falls, in a high measure spoken in the street's own words: the grand line and the plain word side by side. Let a line stretch by a beat or two where the song's joke or mockery lands. Keep the song's holy things and its low things in the same breath, as the song has them; add no place, no joke and no patter of your own. The refrain comes back word for word, ringing like a call to the crowd, and the signature couplet sets the singer's name where the rhyme falls if it can, keeping 'says'.
lenses.why: The gleeman signs his song inside it ('Gather round poor Zozimus, yer friend') as the siddha does ('Lūyī says'), and carries a whole book in memory. He sets the high couplet against the street's speech, as the siddhas put the highest truth in the lowest terms.
lenses.touchstone: Ye sons and daughters of Erin, attend, / Gather round poor Zozimus, yer friend;
lenses.suits: the mocking songs, the songs against pious show, a signature that must ring

lenses.name: Hermit lyric
lenses.after: after the early Irish nature quatrains (8th–10th centuries): the blackbird over Belfast Lough, the scribe under the hedge of trees
lenses.how: Very short lines, one to each half-line, each closed. Every thing the song names made exact in colour and sound, heard before it is seen where the song's order allows; a name may wait to the end of its line. No moral, and no 'I' the song lacks. Chime inside the line: the same vowel, the same first consonant. The refrain stays word for word, and the signature keeps 'says'.
lenses.why: Meyer: 'the half-said thing to them is dearest'. These are the Irish twins of the Zen mountain poems, and they give a caryā image the cool clarity it has before any reading is put on it.
lenses.touchstone: A hedge of trees surrounds me, / A blackbird's lay sings to me
lenses.suits: the nature images, the bird, the boat on the water, any one thing seen

lenses.name: Aisling
lenses.after: after the vision poems of Aogán Ó Rathaille and the song-poets (c. 1700–1800)
lenses.how: Long lines of four or five stresses, one to each half-line, with the same vowel in the same stressed places line after line (the song-poets' stress-frame). Where the song meets a figure (Ḍombī at the edge of town), describe her part by part in the song's own words, and where the song doubles a word, double it (brightness of brightness). What she stands for is never said in the line: the reading stays in the notes. The refrain stays word for word, and the signature keeps 'says'.
lenses.why: The aisling is a twilight language: love on the surface, a hidden allegiance beneath. It is the test of the edition's rule that readings go in the notes and the line keeps its strangeness.
lenses.touchstone: The Brightness of Brightness I saw in a lonely path
lenses.suits: Ḍombī, the woman met at the edge of town, the songs read two ways
